value.overview: The Chimney Swift (Chaetura pelagica) is a small, highly aerial swift that breeds in eastern North America and migrates to South America. It spends most of its life flying, catching insects above towns, forests, wetlands, rivers, and agricultural areas. Its narrow, curved wings, cigar-shaped body, stiff wingbeats, and rapid chattering call make it distinctive. Unlike most birds, it cannot perch and instead clings to vertical surfaces inside chimneys, tree cavities, caves, and similar structures.
value.classification: The Chimney Swift belongs to the order Apodiformes and the swift family Apodidae. It is a monotypic species, with no currently recognized subspecies.
value.identification: This small swift is about 12–15 cm long, with a wingspan of roughly 27–30 cm. It has a slender, tube-shaped body, very long and narrow curved wings, a short tapered tail, and a tiny bill. Its plumage is dark gray-brown overall, with a slightly paler throat. In flight it shows rapid, stiff wingbeats, frequent banking and twisting, and little flexing at the wrists. Its high, chattering calls are commonly heard while it is flying.
value.rangeHabitat: The Chimney Swift breeds across much of the eastern United States and southern Canada, especially in towns, suburbs, and other areas with suitable chimneys. It also uses hollow trees, caves, and other enclosed vertical spaces. During migration it forages over forests, fields, wetlands, rivers, lakes, and urban areas. In Costa Rica it is a passage migrant, occurring particularly along the Caribbean side during spring and autumn migration. Large feeding flocks may gather over open areas, especially during unsettled or stormy weather; it is not normally a resident breeding species there.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Chimney Swifts pass through Costa Rica mainly from mid-March to late April and from early October to early November, generally continuing south to wintering areas in the upper Amazon basin rather than remaining in Costa Rica through the winter.
value.breeding: Breeding occurs mainly from late spring through summer in eastern North America. A pair builds a small half-cup nest from short twigs cemented to an interior vertical surface with glue-like saliva. Traditional brick chimneys are important nesting sites, but hollow trees, caves, wells, air shafts, and other enclosed structures may also be used. The species usually nests as a single pair, although an unmated adult may sometimes help. Incubation lasts about 16–21 days, and young leave the nest roughly 14–19 days after hatching.
value.dietFeeding: Chimney Swifts feed almost entirely on flying insects and other small airborne arthropods, including beetles, flies, ants, wasps, true bugs, and moths. They capture prey in continuous flight, often feeding high above water, forest edges, fields, and developed areas. They may forage alone or in loose flocks and sometimes associate with swallows and other swifts. Their dependence on abundant flying insects makes them sensitive to changes in insect availability and aerial habitat quality.
value.behavior: This is one of North America’s most aerial birds. It normally flies throughout the day except when nesting or roosting, and it rarely lands on horizontal surfaces. Chimney Swifts communicate with rapid chattering calls, bathe by touching the water while flying, and gather communally in chimneys or other enclosed roosts during migration. Large flocks may circle above a roost at dusk before funneling inside. Their small feet and stiff tail are adapted for clinging to vertical walls rather than perching.

conservation.populationTrend: Declining. North American monitoring indicates a severe cumulative reduction since the mid-20th century, with continuing declines in recent decades. In Costa Rica, it is a seasonal migrant rather than a breeding resident, so local numbers mainly reflect migration conditions and the health of populations along the full migration route.
conservation.threats: Loss of suitable nesting and roosting sites is a major threat, especially as old masonry chimneys deteriorate, are capped, or are replaced by modern structures with unsuitable interiors. Loss of hollow trees and forest habitat may also reduce natural sites. Additional concerns include declines in flying insects, pesticide exposure, habitat degradation along migration routes, and possible loss of wintering habitat through logging and fires in the Amazon basin.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect active nests and roosts, and avoid chimney repair, cleaning, capping, or demolition while swifts are present. Maintain suitable unused masonry chimneys where safe, or provide purpose-built swift towers. Preserve mature trees, forest edges, wetlands, rivers, and open areas that support flying insects. Reduce unnecessary pesticide use, support habitat conservation in Costa Rica and the Amazon basin, and report sightings and migration flocks to reputable bird-monitoring programs.
